These notes outline a highly structured, iterative software development framework you're calling Evolutionary Modular Dimensional TDD. It is designed to tackle complex growth through rapid iteration, distinct development phases, and strategic testing.

Here is a high-level architectural overview of the methodology detailed across your files, breaking down the mechanics of your "Tracer Round" waves.

I. Motivation and The Core Philosophy

As outlined in 11378.jpg, the foundation of this system is built on rapid iteration and pushing past operational friction ("Don't be afraid to begin anew").

  • The Emotional Vector: You noted a transition from feeling "sad" (not paying attention) to "angry," which serves as a catalyst for action (fighting back, doing something) when comfort and safety are removed.
  • Handoffs & Formalization: You recognized a need to formalize your process. Good tests equate to "Good Growth Waves."
  • Multi-Dimensional Testing: Rather than a simple pass/fail bar, you're designing tests on a gradient. By grading each dimension independently and combining them into a final report (visualized as a radar chart), you create a robust testing suite that accommodates ranges and tolerances.

II. The "Tracer Round" Wave Architecture

11379.jpg and 11380.jpg define the granular mechanics of the development cycle. The process is divided into strict, repeating phases to prevent complex growth from becoming unmanageable: {Growth Phase} -> {Document Phase} -> {Oversight / Rearchitecture / Planning} -> {Repeat}.

  • Role Separation:
    • Driver: Handles the initial R&D and drives the code.
    • Thinker/Mapper/Secondary: Generates documentation, connects systems, and architects the coarse and fine-level understanding (the "Collage Report").
  • Wave Mechanics:
    • Reconnaissance: Initial experimental tracers are used purely for research to "uncover the map" and categorize outcomes into Good (Works), Bad (Does not work), and Ugly (Oh boy).
    • Breakpoints: Once a wave reaches a breakpoint (pass or fail), the tracer is documented via After Action Reports (AAR), and the codebase is purged for the next wave.
    • Refinement: After a problem is solved, development stops. You go back to refine, create deep documentation, build libraries, brainstorm, and re-architect—even switching to more performant languages like C, C++, Rust, or Go if necessary.
  • AI Integration: You explicitly map out a flow where a "Wave I Report" is fed into a "Gemini Next Draft Tracers" process to assist in generating the subsequent testing suite and knowledge expressions.

III. Testing & Branching Strategy

11381.jpg establishes the rules for how testing and documentation live within the version control system.

  • Independence: Testing is treated independently from development and documentation.
  • Evolution of Tests: End-to-end tests are favored during the early "tracer rounds," while full unit-testing is reserved for late-stage hardening.
  • Branching Schema: Testing and documentation begin alongside the program but eventually move to their own dedicated branches or microservices. They can then be selectively merged back into the main branch via specific files or sub-directories as needed.
  • Data Quality: Better testing requires diverse data inputs—mocks, simulated data, heuristic modeling, and understanding the exact ratios of data required to stress-test the system effectively.

This is a rigorous, deeply process-oriented framework that enforces necessary pauses for architectural mapping before diving back into the code.
